title: From stakeholder analysis to a communication plan
blurb: Explain how stakeholder analysis tells you who needs what, when, how and from whom, and turn it into a communication management plan.
question: A rail operator is upgrading a busy commuter station. The project manager has drafted a communication plan that sends the same monthly report to everyone, but no stakeholder analysis has been done. Why is this plan unlikely to be effective, and how should stakeholder analysis shape it?

teach.body: A communication management plan sets out who needs what information, why they need it, when and how often, in what format and through which channel, who will send it, and how feedback will be gathered. Stakeholder analysis is what fills that plan in. It identifies the stakeholders and assesses their interest, power or influence, attitude and needs. In plain English: you can't decide what to tell people, or how, until you know who they are and what they care about.

teach.caption: Every row comes from the analysis. Feedback routes (app comments, Q&A, a liaison number) are part of the plan too.

teach.body: If the analysis is weak, the plan goes wrong in predictable ways: powerful people get detail they ignore, interested people are left out, opponents receive one-way messages that harden their views, and nobody owns key messages. Stakeholders also change: people move roles, new groups appear and attitudes shift as the project moves through its phases. So the analysis is refreshed regularly and the plan, a living document, is updated with it.

teach.h: How the plan looks in each life cycle

rows.label: When written
values: In Definition, part of the PMP

teach.caption: Either way, the content of the plan still comes from analysing who needs what.

teach.text: Two classic distractors: 'copy everyone into everything for transparency' (that is information overload, not a plan) and 'write the plan once at initiation and keep it fixed'. The order is always analysis first, plan second, and both are repeated as stakeholders change.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: State what a communication management plan sets out: who, what, why, when and how often, format and channel, from whom, feedback.
Explain that stakeholder analysis (interest, power or influence, attitude, needs) supplies those answers.
Give a specific link, e.g. high power but low interest means short summaries timed to decisions.
Note that attitude shapes tone and sender: opponents need two-way, face-to-face contact.
Finish with why it matters: the plan is reviewed and updated as the analysis changes.
The plan answers: who, what, why, when and how often, format and channel, from whom, and how feedback is gathered.
Stakeholder analysis (interest, power or influence, attitude, needs) provides those answers.
Power/interest grid: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor.
Weak analysis gives irrelevant, mistimed or one-way messages.
Both the analysis and the plan are living: revisit them as stakeholders and phases change.

summary: You can now explain how stakeholder analysis drives every part of a communication management plan, from content and channel to timing and sender. You can also explain why the plan must be refreshed whenever the analysis changes, in linear and iterative projects alike.

A.q: Complete the statement: a communication management plan is most effective when it is based on…
options: the sponsor's preferred reporting format
a standard template used on every project
an analysis of each stakeholder's needs
the frequency set by the project board
A.why: The plan should be built from stakeholder analysis, so each group gets the information it needs, in a form and at a time that suits it.

whyNot.0: The sponsor's preference matters for the sponsor, but other stakeholders have different needs.
whyNot.1: A standard template can help structure the plan, but its content must come from analysing this project's stakeholders.
whyNot.3: Frequency should follow stakeholder needs, not a single figure imposed for everyone.

A.q: Which set of questions should a communication management plan answer for each stakeholder or group?
options: Who, what, why, when, how, and from whom
What scope, at what cost, and by when
Who is responsible, accountable, consulted
Which risks, how likely, and how severe
A.why: The plan records who needs what information, why, when and how often, in what format and channel, from whom, and how feedback is gathered.

whyNot.1: Scope, cost and time are the subject of the scope, budget and schedule, not the communication plan.
whyNot.2: Responsible, accountable, consulted (and informed) is a RACI chart for assigning roles to work.
whyNot.3: Likelihood and severity are risk assessment questions for the risk register.

A.q: Stakeholder analysis for an office move shows the finance director has high power but little interest in day-to-day detail. What should the communication plan provide for them?
options: Daily detailed progress emails
Membership of the weekly team stand-up
No updates unless they request them
Brief summaries at key decision points
A.why: High power, low interest means 'keep satisfied': concise, high-level information timed to the decisions where their power matters.

whyNot.0: Daily detail suits a high-interest stakeholder; it will be ignored and may irritate this one.
whyNot.1: Stand-ups are working sessions for the delivery team, not the right forum for a busy senior stakeholder.
whyNot.2: Leaving a powerful stakeholder uninformed risks a surprise objection that could stop the project.

B.q: A project manager writes a communication plan before carrying out any stakeholder analysis. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The plan will be quicker to approve by the board
Messages may miss the needs of key stakeholders
Stakeholders will receive no information at all
The plan cannot be included in the project plan
B.why: Without analysis the plan is guesswork: content, timing and channels may not match what stakeholders actually need, and some may be missed entirely.

whyNot.0: Speed of approval isn't the issue; an unfounded plan is simply less effective.
whyNot.2: Information will still be sent, just not necessarily the right information to the right people.
whyNot.3: It can still sit in the project management plan; the problem is its quality, not where it is filed.

B.q: Midway through a housing project, a new residents' association forms and opposes the scheme. What should happen to the communication plan?
options: Keep it unchanged, since it was baselined at the start
Pass the association's concerns to the sponsor only
Add the association to the weekly newsletter list
Re-analyse the association, then update the plan
B.why: A new, opposed stakeholder needs analysing (power, interest, attitude, needs) so the plan can set suitable, probably two-way, communication with them.

whyNot.0: The plan is a living document; leaving it unchanged ignores a significant new stakeholder.
whyNot.1: Escalating may be part of the response, but the plan still needs to cover how the project communicates with the group.
whyNot.2: A one-way newsletter is unlikely to address an opposed group's concerns, and it skips the analysis step.

B.q: Analysis shows warehouse staff are anxious about, and resistant to, a new automated picking system. Which approach should the plan specify for them?
options: Two-way face-to-face sessions to hear concerns
A monthly written report on the project budget
Notices on the staff board once it is installed
An email from IT setting out the technical design
B.why: A resistant, anxious attitude calls for interactive communication where concerns can be heard and answered, ideally from a trusted sender.

whyNot.1: Budget reports don't address what worries staff and give no chance to respond.
whyNot.2: Telling them after installation is too late and one-way, which feeds resistance.
whyNot.3: Technical detail from IT doesn't match their needs and doesn't invite dialogue.

C.q:
Which THREE of the following should a communication management plan record?
1. What information each stakeholder needs
2. Who is responsible for issuing it
3. Each team member's salary band
4. How feedback will be gathered
options: 1, 2 and 3
1, 3 and 4
1, 2 and 4
2, 3 and 4
C.why: The plan covers what information is needed, who sends it and how feedback is gathered (along with why, when, how often, format and channel).

whyNot.0: Salary bands are confidential HR information, not part of a communication plan.
whyNot.1: This includes salary bands and leaves out who is responsible for issuing each message.
whyNot.3: This includes salary bands and leaves out what information each stakeholder needs.

C.q: On an iterative software project, business users feel out of touch between releases. Analysis shows they value seeing working features far more than reading reports. Which change to the plan is best?
options: Send them the full sprint backlog as a weekly email
Invite them to the end-of-iteration demonstrations
Give them a detailed written report at each gate
Ask them to read the team's daily stand-up minutes
C.why: The analysis says they value seeing working features, so the plan should bring them to the iteration reviews, which are interactive and show real progress.

whyNot.0: A backlog email is still a written document, which the analysis says they don't value.
whyNot.2: Gate reports belong to a linear rhythm and are written, so they ignore the stated preference.
whyNot.3: Stand-up notes are internal team detail and are still something to read.

C.q: Which is NOT a sound reason for revisiting the communication management plan?
options: A key stakeholder has changed role
The project has moved into its next phase of work
Feedback shows updates are misunderstood
The PM wants one report format for everyone
C.why: A single format for all ignores differing stakeholder needs; that is the opposite of what a plan based on analysis should do.

whyNot.0: A new person in a key role may have different interests and preferences, so the analysis and plan should be refreshed.
whyNot.1: Information needs change between phases, so a phase change is a natural point to review the plan.
whyNot.2: Feedback showing misunderstanding is exactly the signal that content, format or channel needs adjusting.

reteach.title: Planning who hears what about a wedding
reteach.question: A couple are planning their wedding. Why wouldn't they send exactly the same message, in the same way, to the grandparents, the friends, the caterer and the venue?

blocks.h: Know your guests before you write
blocks.body: Before sending anything, the couple think about each group. Grandparents want a printed invitation and a phone call, and have strong views on the ceremony. Friends live on a group chat. The caterer needs exact numbers and dietary needs by a deadline. The venue needs final timings in writing. That thinking is stakeholder analysis. The list of who gets what, when, how and from whom is the communication plan.

blocks.h: From the guest list to the message

children.label: Grandparents
children.sub: Printed invite and a call, from the couple

children.label: Friends
children.sub: Group chat updates, from the best man

children.label: Caterer
children.sub: Numbers and diets, in writing, by a deadline

children.label: Venue
children.sub: Final timings, signed off, two weeks ahead

blocks.caption: Each branch answers who, what, how, when and from whom, because the couple thought about each group first.

blocks.text: If the couple had sent one group email to everyone, the caterer would lack detail, the grandparents might never see it, and friends would be flooded with logistics. Same message for all is the sign of a plan with no analysis behind it.

explain.body: A communication management plan records, for each stakeholder or group: what information they need and why, when and how often, in what format and through which channel, who is responsible for sending it, and how feedback will be gathered. It sits within the project management plan and is owned by the project manager.

letters.word: How: format and channel, from whom

test.q: Which element is included in a communication plan so the project manager can tell whether messages are actually being understood?
options: How feedback is gathered
Who is responsible for sending
Which channel is used
How often it is sent
test.why: Planned feedback routes (questions, surveys, review meetings) show whether messages are landing as intended.

whyNot.1: Ownership makes sure messages are sent, not that they are understood.
whyNot.2: The channel affects reach, but on its own it doesn't tell you about understanding.
whyNot.3: Frequency controls timing, not whether the message is understood.

explain.body: Stakeholder analysis looks at each stakeholder's interest in the project, their power or influence over it, their attitude (supportive, neutral or opposed) and their needs. Each one feeds a different part of the plan: needs shape content and format, interest and power shape depth and frequency, and attitude shapes tone, sender and how two-way the contact must be.

test.q: Which analysis finding most directly tells the project manager to plan two-way, persuasive communication rather than simple information updates?
options: The stakeholder has low interest
The stakeholder is based overseas
The stakeholder is strongly opposed
The stakeholder needs brief reports
test.why: Attitude drives tone and interaction: an opposed stakeholder needs dialogue so their concerns can be heard and addressed.

whyNot.0: Low interest suggests lighter-touch updates, not persuasion.
whyNot.1: Location affects channel and timing, not whether persuasion is needed.
whyNot.3: Needing brief reports affects format and detail, not the need for dialogue.

explain.body: Mapping stakeholders by power and interest gives a quick steer. Manage closely (high power, high interest): frequent, two-way, involved in decisions. Keep satisfied (high power, low interest): concise and timed to decisions. Keep informed (low power, high interest): regular updates and a way to ask questions. Monitor (low, low): light-touch updates, watching for change.

test.q: Local residents next to a construction site are very interested in the works but have little power over the project. Using a power/interest grid, how should they be treated?
options: Manage closely
Keep informed
Keep satisfied
Monitor only
test.why: High interest with low power places them in 'keep informed': regular updates and a clear way to raise questions.

whyNot.0: Manage closely is for stakeholders with both high power and high interest.
whyNot.2: Keep satisfied is for high power but low interest.
whyNot.3: Monitor is for low power and low interest; these residents are highly interested.

explain.h: A living plan in any life cycle
explain.body: People change jobs, new groups emerge and attitudes harden or soften, so the analysis is repeated and the plan updated. In a linear project the plan is written in Definition, held in the project management plan and reviewed at each gate. In an iterative project it is lighter and built around the team's rhythm of stand-ups, reviews and retrospectives, and it is revisited as iterations end.

test.q: Why should the stakeholder analysis and communication plan be revisited throughout a project?
options: The sponsor must re-sign it every week
The PMP needs a new template each phase
Iterative projects ban any fixed plans
Stakeholders and their needs change
test.why: Stakeholders, their attitudes and their information needs change over the life of a project, so the plan must keep pace.

whyNot.0: There's no requirement for weekly re-signing; the point is keeping the content relevant.
whyNot.1: Templates are not the reason; the content must reflect current stakeholders.
whyNot.2: Iterative projects still plan communication; they just keep the plan lighter and review it often.
